值得閱讀的理由

  • 從長年 Apple 使用者的角度，檢視觸控 MacBook Pro 與摺疊 iPhone 是否帶來真正創新。
  • 比較 Apple 過往「雖然晚到，卻重新定義產品」的做法，與作者眼中如今缺乏突破的落差。
  • 探討品牌忠誠、產品溢價與生態系依賴，如何影響消費者對 Apple 的信任。

摘要

期待已久的觸控 Mac，帶來了什麼？

作者先說明，這不是開箱或新聞整理，而是自己使用 iPhone Duo、看到新款觸控 MacBook Pro 後的個人感想；影片也由 iPhone Duo 拍攝。身為使用 Apple 超過二十年的老用戶，作者打算從觸控 Mac、摺疊 iPhone，以及品牌近年的產品風格談起。

多年來，消費者期待 Apple 讓 iPad 擁有完整的 Mac 式多工能力，或讓 Mac 支援觸控與 Apple Pencil，成為能取代多種裝置的二合一產品。然而，iPadOS 與 macOS 仍被區隔，iPad 上的應用程式往往是功能較精簡的版本，即使 iPad 採用與 Mac 相同的 M 系列晶片，也未能充分發揮生產力。

如今 Apple 終於推出觸控 Mac，作者原本期待這些年等待是為了找到更出色的操作方式，沒想到實際呈現卻與其他觸控 PC 相似：使用者仍得抬手點按螢幕，許多應用程式也未針對觸控最佳化。它既不支援 Apple Pencil，也不能拆下或大幅翻折成平板，作者因此認為，等了多年得到的只是遲來且缺乏獨特性的設計。

摺疊 iPhone 也沒有展現獨到之處

談到 iPhone Duo，作者原先以為 Apple 遲遲不推出摺疊手機，是在克服耐用度、軟體適配等難題，並準備展示不同於其他摺疊機的使用方式。但發表會沒有呈現這種突破；內螢幕的摺痕只是以霧面保護貼遮掩，軟體體驗也未見特別之處。

作者也曾期待 Apple 把鉸鏈與螢幕結構做得更可靠，然而他提到已有螢幕損壞的案例，並指出拆解資訊顯示，內部設計並未展現革命性的耐用方案。即使防水防塵標示亮眼，細沙與毛髮仍可能進入機身。作者認為，無論軟體或硬體，iPhone Duo 都沒有重新發明摺疊手機，只像是在相似產品上加上 Apple 標誌，並可能以更高價格出售。

遲到並非問題，缺乏理由才是

作者強調，Apple 過去也不是許多產品的先行者：iPod、iPhone 與 iPad 都不是同類產品中的第一款；但 iPhone 曾整合多種功能，讓手機更方便使用，並帶動產業改變。過往 Apple 即使晚到，仍能提出足以改變市場的解法；如今觸控 Mac 與摺疊 iPhone 卻沒有帶來同等程度的創新，讓作者感覺 Apple 只是沒有充分理由地遲到。

作者以一位總是遲到的朋友作比喻：從前對方會有令人信服的理由，如今卻像是認為多年交情足以讓人原諒。Apple 長期累積的信任，使粉絲願意為產品支付溢價，期待品牌早已替他們想好更好的解決方案；但現在，額外付出的錢似乎只換來標誌，或反映出使用者受限於生態系而難以離開。

逐漸消磨的品牌信任

使用 Apple 二十多年的作者坦言，最令人擔心的是信任正在變薄。當 Apple 展示觸控 Mac 上的點按與拖曳時，他不禁質疑這與多年來其他 PC 的做法有何不同；而發表會的呈現方式，卻常讓人感覺這些功能彷彿是全新的發明。影片最後談到這種產品宣傳所形成的氛圍，但字幕在句子尚未結束時便中斷。

Hey everyone, this video is neither an unboxing nor a news recap; it’s just me sharing some thoughts after using the iPhone Duo and seeing the new touchscreen MacBook Pro. You might wonder, why don't I have the iPhone Duo in my hand? Because we’re actually using the iPhone Duo to film this right now, so you can also get a look at how its camera performs. The following video will contain a lot of my own personal, subjective opinions as an Apple fan of over 20 years. If you’re used to watching our videos for news or leaks, this one isn’t like that, so feel free to keep watching if you’re interested. I’ll be breaking this video down into a few parts. First, we’ll talk about this. touchscreen MacBook Pro—after waiting all these years, what did we actually get? Second, we’ll discuss the iPhone Duo and why I feel the form factor of these products and Apple's recent style feel almost exactly the same. In the final sections, I’ll share my own conclusions and thoughts, and of course , I hope you’ll join the discussion. Let’s get started. Right, let's start with this touchscreen MacBook Pro, as everyone has been waiting years for Apple to finally release a Mac that you can touch. Actually, people had different expectations; we either hoped for a Pad that could unlock the multitasking capabilities of a Mac, or for a Mac with a touchscreen that. supports Apple Pencil, allowing it to handle all the use cases an iPad can. No matter the direction, it’s about a true two-in-one device, so you don't have to carry an extra device just for specific functions. So, at first, we saw Apple finally unlock iPadOS, giving it more multitasking. capabilities, and slowly expanding into different usage modes. You can connect an external monitor, plug in a keyboard and mouse, and have a desktop-like usage experience. However, even though we know how powerful the processors in an iPad are, Apple still intentionally uses iPadOS to suppress. much of its true productivity. It ends up being that if you want to use many apps, they are split between two different environments, and even for some professional apps, you might have to navigate two separate environments. Even if you don't have to buy them twice , the apps you use on a Pad will always be simplified versions of those on a Mac . Even today, the user experience we get on macOS and iPadOS is still vastly different. It’s not just about one supporting touch and the other not; it’s that Apple keeps these two worlds separate. Even when using the same app, you have to tolerate the iPad version being stripped of features. Yet, you.

know there’s no real reason for it to be crippled, given that the iPad uses the same M-series processors as the Mac. Fast forward to today, and we’ve kind of given up on the idea of the iPad being fully unleashed. Apple has finally launched a Mac with a touchscreen. After waiting so long, our expectation was that Apple avoided touchscreens for years because they were seeking a better solution, spending all that time reinventing and researching to show the world that while Apple might be late, we always do it best—and to tell everyone that our approach changes the entire. industry. Unfortunately, after such a long wait, the result we see is exactly the same as other PCs. The way the touchscreen works is identical, and there are even many apps that haven’t been optimized for this touch mode at all. Not to mention, even if all the apps on the Mac were optimized for touch , the design remains the same as any PC . You have to lift your arm to tap the screen, which is something PCs have been doing for many years. And that’s not even considering the lack of stylus or Apple Pencil support on the Mac, nor. does it compare to some PCs that have screens that detach or fold all the way back to become a true tablet. For use cases like drawing or other touch-based tasks, those designs feel much more logical. But the newly released MacBook Pro lacks these features, and I believe it's an intentional choice by Apple. Waiting 16 years only to see Apple release this makes me think, "Steve Jobs was right." Because we see that Apple waited this long, only to launch a product that contradicts what Steve Jobs previously said—that such a touch interface is meaningless—without giving anyone a good reason as to why they decided to do it now. So what we’re left with is a product that is very late to. the game. It’s finally here, but it’s identical to what everyone else has been offering for the past decade. Let’s use Apple as an example: they’re like a good friend of yours. In the past, whenever they were late, they’d always give you a great reason—maybe they helped an elderly person cross the street, or stopped to assist at a car accident. But over time, they’ve started showing up later and later, acting like nothing happened without even an apology. Sometimes there isn't even an excuse; they just overslept, thinking, "You guys won't get mad anyway, so it doesn't matter if I'm a jerk." Moving on to the iPhone Duo, I’m seeing the exact same.

pattern here. We’ve waited so many years , and while I initially thought foldable phones weren’t practical, we assumed it was due to durability concerns or perhaps optimization issues. Or maybe they spent all those years just trying to perfect the best way to use a foldable, so we waited until now, thinking Apple was finally unveiling something special. I spent the entire presentation waiting for Apple to showcase the iPhone Duo, hoping they’d reveal a unique use case—whether in hardware or software—that would truly set them apart from other foldables and make us feel like they had reinvented the device. Unfortunately, the entire. presentation didn't show that at all. They used a matte screen protector to hide the crease, so once you take that off, the inner screen is essentially the same as everyone else's, even in terms of software application. Leaks about this foldable have been circulating for a long time—I’ve even been talking about it for two years. I was hoping that since Apple was finally launching it, they’d have a better solution for how the inner and outer screens integrate. Clearly, there isn't one. Then, I find myself making excuses for Apple again, thinking, "Fine, maybe the software needs time, but surely they’ve figured out the hardware engineering to make the. hinge super durable, solving all the issues other foldables have." It would be reasonable to think they waited so long just to get the foundation right. But that’s not the case either. We’re already seeing a bunch of reports about the screen breaking entirely due to their poor design. Many people haven't even dropped their phones, and while Apple might replace them for minor issues, we've seen many teardowns of the internal hinge design, and Apple hasn't really found a more revolutionary or durable way to do it. The water and dust resistance ratings are labeled very high , yet fine sand and hair can still get. in at any time. Looking back at it, whether in terms of software or hardware for foldables, Apple hasn't reinvented anything at all; it’s all the same, just slapping an Apple logo on the same product and likely charging a lot more than everyone else. So, coming back to our opening question: Apple joined the game years late, and us long-time fans used to expect that they were spending the time to solve problems no one else could, ready to revolutionize the market again, right? But after using it and seeing the current Mac announcements, the simple answer is that Apple hasn't done any of that. So it's hard not to think that Apple today is just trying to find more ways to sell nostalgia through.

their logo, expanding a bunch of new product lines just to make a bit more money. This time, they combined nostalgia with the logo by bringing back the glowing one, which I personally love , but is this the only innovation after all this time? But I want to be clear: my issue isn't with being late. I don't think being late has ever been Apple's problem. They weren't the first to invent a player, the iPhone wasn't the first smartphone or even the first touchscreen phone, and the iPad wasn't the first tablet, so Apple's issue was never about being late; it's just that every time they were late before, they had a very valid reason. Take the iPhone. ; it was a true three-in-one device that combined all those functions to make it more portable and actually easier to use , and we saw it truly revolutionize and lead the entire industry in a new direction. But this time? Touchscreen Macs have been around for over a decade , and we haven't seen any revolutionary applications for Apple's version. And finally, when they release a foldable iPhone without reinventing either software or hardware, they're just like that friend who overslept—late for no reason, simply out of a lack of respect for you. And if you get angry, they use nostalgia and years of friendship to win you over. We were willing to pay a. premium because after waiting so long, we’d get an Apple product and find they had already thought of the solution for us. But now, I feel like the extra money I pay just buys a logo, or is because I’m trapped in the ecosystem and have no choice. Honestly, that’s what worries me the most. Having used Apple products for over 20 years, I’ve always trusted their track record, believing that even if Apple was late, they always did it best . That kind of trust is built generation by generation, but after all these years , it’s started to wear thin. There are times when things feel really underwhelming, like when they demo what a touchscreen MacBook Pro can do. They’re up there tapping and dragging, and I’m thinking, fine, but how is this any different from what PCs have been doing for the last decade? With every Apple product launch, a parallel universe seems to emerge. So many people share it as if it’s the first time the world has ever seen such a thing, and the whole sentiment feels like the creation of some kind of cult-like dimension. Of course, as a fan, I sometimes get swept up in the hype myself, so I have to take some of the responsibility. But if we were to simply say Apple has lost its creativity, I think that’s an oversimplification. How could a brand with the highest market value and the most money in the consumer product space, with all their talent, be.

incapable of innovation? So, is it a leadership issue, or have they fundamentally changed their direction? The new person has only been in charge for a month, and given that product planning and development take at least three to five years, I don’t think we can fully judge the current product lineup as representing their intended future direction. So, we won’t jump to conclusions just yet. Instead, let’s look at the current products and compare them to previous lineups to see what Apple is actually trying to achieve by segmenting everything into so many different specs. We’ve mentioned the deliberate limitations of iPadOS, the. years of waiting for macOS touch support , and now the iPhone Duo, which unfolds into an iPad Mini-sized device but runs iOS. You might expect a 2-in-1 device to offer the multitasking or workstation-like usage scenarios you want, or even run those professional apps found on the iPad—but sorry, it’s just an iPhone. Now we see that the newly released iPad mini has finally upgraded to an L-series chip, yet it’s still locked at 60Hz, keeping 120Hz exclusive to the iPad Pro. From my perspective, I feel like they are building their own moats across every product category and every market tier. And I think this is very similar to Apple’s overall external business model. . Like the App Store moat, the old AirDrop moat—which was eventually bypassed—and even more directly, not allowing many third-party devices to pair easily. Honestly, we could go on and on about this forever. To be fair, in some ways, I can understand the need to build a moat to protect the interests of your own products. Apple claims it’s for privacy or to ensure maximum compatibility between their own devices , blocking third-party accessories that wouldn't even be affected by an open system, all to ensure consumers keep buying their products—no matter the excuse. But I feel it has reached a point where it's borderline obsessive; I. often run into these deliberate, ridiculous hardware segmentations even between their own products, and it happens every single day. It’s not just hardware specifications they deliberately segment; even when it's clearly just a software issue, they intentionally cut off features to create as much user inconvenience as possible, all to protect their individual product lines. If these inconveniences can push you to buy another product, they will absolutely do it; even if the software is capable of it, why would they ever give you those features for free? If you.

really want them, just go buy another device. It seems to me like Apple is afraid that if the iPhone were fully unlocked, it would be as powerful as the iPad, causing people to stop buying iPads, so they rush to castrate multitasking software and Apple Pencil Pro features. You're so afraid that if the iPad mini had 120Hz, people wouldn't buy the iPad Pro, so even after a major update, we still have to leave that 120Hz out. And you're afraid that if the iPad had Mac-like multitasking and software capabilities, people wouldn't buy Macs anymore. Even when you put the exact same processor into the iPad, you still use iPadOS to deliberately impose all sorts of restrictions and. limitations. You're afraid that if the Mac gets a touchscreen, nobody will buy an iPad. So, after waiting over a decade for a touchscreen Mac, you deliberately prevent it from being detached, restrict the opening angle to that of a standard laptop to stop it from being used as a tablet, and cut support for the Apple Pencil—forcing anyone who really needs to draw or wants a tablet to go out and buy another device. So, does everyone see this pattern? Of course, every company has to consider its business interests, and I don't see an issue with that. But when business interests become the sole focus, innovation stops, because it seems you're worried that innovation will hurt your existing. profits. Let’s talk about AI. We saw them launch Siri very early on, so they had this vision long ago that a smart voice assistant could theoretically handle many tasks just by you saying a single sentence. But it has stagnated for a very, very long time. Why? Because looking at the way AI works now, it’s not just about simple cloud processing; its use case is somewhat like Apple's Siri combined with their internal Shortcuts app. So, once it can see all the functions within your first-party or third-party apps, as long as it understands what you're saying, it can. complete these tasks for you with just one command. We see that Apple actually has these features on your phone, and you knew very early on that this form of utility could save us a lot of time. But now you're making features so complex that it takes forever to find a simple setting. With every new iOS update, because there are so many settings, you start hiding a bunch of them inside the Accessibility menu, which is extremely difficult to use. A huge problem is that when you ask Siri something, it often has no idea, and as I mentioned, if you use AI, you know that with these methods , we often don't need to operate the.

computer at all, and there's no need to even open a bunch of software or apps. So looking back at this, you realize that when Apple was initially creating Siri and these Shortcuts, they may have already foreseen what would happen once this capability to link everything together became so powerful. First, the massive profits from their App Store would be instantly impacted. Aside from some entertainment-based apps that might still survive, productivity or utility-focused apps would basically become unnecessary. Apple currently generates a huge portion of its revenue from the App Store and these service-based products. Whether it's first-party or third-party subscriptions. , Apple takes a cut from almost all of them. This makes me wonder if Apple's lag in AI, or its delay in integrating features like voice assistants, is really just because they were slow to react? Or is it intentional? They might feel that if this technology becomes too powerful, it could hurt their bottom line. As long as they can delay its development, they can keep earning easy money for a little longer. I don't know what you all think; which direction do you think it is? So, the only thing we can hope for now is that perhaps when a new CEO takes over, they will bring a different direction to lead Apple toward more innovation. Plus, in today's AI. world, Apple is facing a lot of threats . Could these situations force them to start innovating more and refine their products and services? That, for one, is what I look forward to seeing. Otherwise , it's really hard to say. With the current speed of AI advancement, I’m not sure how much longer I can tolerate having to manually open apps, click around, and search for things just to get tasks done. OK, that was a quick rundown of my thoughts for today. I'll wrap the video up here. What do you all...

The following video will contain a lot of my own personal, subjective opinions as an Apple fan of over 20 years. If you’re used to watching our videos for news or leaks, this one isn’t like that, so feel free to keep watching if you’re interested. I’ll be breaking this video down into a few parts. First, we’ll talk about this. touchscreen MacBook Pro—after waiting all these years, what did we actually get? Second, we’ll discuss the iPhone Duo and why I feel the form factor of these products and Apple's recent style feel almost exactly the same. In the final sections, I’ll share my own conclusions and thoughts, and of course , I hope you’ll join the discussion. Let’s get started. Right, let's start with this touchscreen MacBook Pro, as everyone has been waiting years for Apple to finally release a Mac that you can touch. Actually, people had different expectations; we either hoped for a Pad that could unlock the multitasking capabilities of a Mac, or for a Mac with a touchscreen that. supports Apple Pencil, allowing it to handle all the use cases an iPad can. So, at first, we saw Apple finally unlock iPadOS, giving it more multitasking. capabilities, and slowly expanding into different usage modes. You can connect an external monitor, plug in a keyboard and mouse, and have a desktop-like usage experience. However, even though we know how powerful the processors in an iPad are, Apple still intentionally uses iPadOS to suppress. much of its true productivity. It ends up being that if you want to use many apps, they are split between two different environments, and even for some professional apps, you might have to navigate two separate environments. Even if you don't have to buy them twice , the apps you use on a Pad will always be simplified versions of those on a Mac . Even today, the user experience we get on macOS and iPadOS is still vastly different. It’s not just about one supporting touch and the other not; it’s that Apple keeps these two worlds separate. Even when using the same app, you have to tolerate the iPad version being stripped of features. Yet, you.

know there’s no real reason for it to be crippled, given that the iPad uses the same M-series processors as the Mac. Fast forward to today, and we’ve kind of given up on the idea of the iPad being fully unleashed. Apple has finally launched a Mac with a touchscreen. After waiting so long, our expectation was that Apple avoided touchscreens for years because they were seeking a better solution, spending all that time reinventing and researching to show the world that while Apple might be late, we always do it best—and to tell everyone that our approach changes the entire. industry. Unfortunately, after such a long wait, the result we see is exactly the same as other PCs. The way the touchscreen works is identical, and there are even many apps that haven’t been optimized for this touch mode at all. Not to mention, even if all the apps on the Mac were optimized for touch , the design remains the same as any PC . You have to lift your arm to tap the screen, which is something PCs have been doing for many years. And that’s not even considering the lack of stylus or Apple Pencil support on the Mac, nor. does it compare to some PCs that have screens that detach or fold all the way back to become a true tablet. For use cases like drawing or other touch-based tasks, those designs feel much more logical. But the newly released MacBook Pro lacks these features, and I believe it's an intentional choice by Apple. Waiting 16 years only to see Apple release this makes me think, "Steve Jobs was right." But over time, they’ve started showing up later and later, acting like nothing happened without even an apology. Sometimes there isn't even an excuse; they just overslept, thinking, "You guys won't get mad anyway, so it doesn't matter if I'm a jerk." Moving on to the iPhone Duo, I’m seeing the exact same.

pattern here. We’ve waited so many years , and while I initially thought foldable phones weren’t practical, we assumed it was due to durability concerns or perhaps optimization issues. incapable of innovation? So, is it a leadership issue, or have they fundamentally changed their direction? really want them, just go buy another device. We see that Apple actually has these features on your phone, and you knew very early on that this form of utility could save us a lot of time. computer at all, and there's no need to even open a bunch of software or apps. 值得閱讀的理由

  • 從長年 Apple 使用者的角度，檢視觸控 MacBook Pro 與摺疊 iPhone 是否帶來真正創新。
  • 比較 Apple 過往「雖然晚到，卻重新定義產品」的做法，與作者眼中如今缺乏突破的落差。
  • 探討品牌忠誠、產品溢價與生態系依賴，如何影響消費者對 Apple 的信任。

摘要

期待已久的觸控 Mac，帶來了什麼？

作者先說明，這不是開箱或新聞整理，而是自己使用 iPhone Duo、看到新款觸控 MacBook Pro 後的個人感想；影片也由 iPhone Duo 拍攝。身為使用 Apple 超過二十年的老用戶，作者打算從觸控 Mac、摺疊 iPhone，以及品牌近年的產品風格談起。

多年來，消費者期待 Apple 讓 iPad 擁有完整的 Mac 式多工能力，或讓 Mac 支援觸控與 Apple Pencil，成為能取代多種裝置的二合一產品。然而，iPadOS 與 macOS 仍被區隔，iPad 上的應用程式往往是功能較精簡的版本，即使 iPad 採用與 Mac 相同的 M 系列晶片，也未能充分發揮生產力。

如今 Apple 終於推出觸控 Mac，作者原本期待這些年等待是為了找到更出色的操作方式，沒想到實際呈現卻與其他觸控 PC 相似：使用者仍得抬手點按螢幕，許多應用程式也未針對觸控最佳化。它既不支援 Apple Pencil，也不能拆下或大幅翻折成平板，作者因此認為，等了多年得到的只是遲來且缺乏獨特性的設計。

摺疊 iPhone 也沒有展現獨到之處

談到 iPhone Duo，作者原先以為 Apple 遲遲不推出摺疊手機，是在克服耐用度、軟體適配等難題，並準備展示不同於其他摺疊機的使用方式。但發表會沒有呈現這種突破；內螢幕的摺痕只是以霧面保護貼遮掩，軟體體驗也未見特別之處。

作者也曾期待 Apple 把鉸鏈與螢幕結構做得更可靠，然而他提到已有螢幕損壞的案例，並指出拆解資訊顯示，內部設計並未展現革命性的耐用方案。即使防水防塵標示亮眼，細沙與毛髮仍可能進入機身。作者認為，無論軟體或硬體，iPhone Duo 都沒有重新發明摺疊手機，只像是在相似產品上加上 Apple 標誌，並可能以更高價格出售。

遲到並非問題，缺乏理由才是

作者強調，Apple 過去也不是許多產品的先行者：iPod、iPhone 與 iPad 都不是同類產品中的第一款；但 iPhone 曾整合多種功能，讓手機更方便使用，並帶動產業改變。過往 Apple 即使晚到，仍能提出足以改變市場的解法；如今觸控 Mac 與摺疊 iPhone 卻沒有帶來同等程度的創新，讓作者感覺 Apple 只是沒有充分理由地遲到。

作者以一位總是遲到的朋友作比喻：從前對方會有令人信服的理由，如今卻像是認為多年交情足以讓人原諒。Apple 長期累積的信任，使粉絲願意為產品支付溢價，期待品牌早已替他們想好更好的解決方案；但現在，額外付出的錢似乎只換來標誌，或反映出使用者受限於生態系而難以離開。

逐漸消磨的品牌信任

使用 Apple 二十多年的作者坦言，最令人擔心的是信任正在變薄。當 Apple 展示觸控 Mac 上的點按與拖曳時，他不禁質疑這與多年來其他 PC 的做法有何不同；而發表會的呈現方式，卻常讓人感覺這些功能彷彿是全新的發明。影片最後談到這種產品宣傳所形成的氛圍，但字幕在句子尚未結束時便中斷。
